name: Sara Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of two full-time workers at Pearce Orchards, sixty hectares of apples and pears, mostly Gala, Bramley for cooking, and Conference pears. In November it's the cold store, the big chilled sheds where the fruit's kept, and grading, then from December it's pruning till March. In autumn it's picking with the seasonal crew, thirty of them, and I help run the bins and the tractor.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love blossom week. The whole place goes white and pink and the bees come in on hired hives, and for about ten days it's the best job in the world. What wears me out is pruning. It's eight hours on a ladder with cold hands, deciding which branch to take off, and I'm still slow at it. Derek, the owner, does a tree in four minutes and I take twelve.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology or AI tools in the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A bit. The cold store has sensors that send Derek alerts if the temperature drifts. I've used a chatbot a couple of times, once to write a complaint to the ladder company and once to check a photo of a leaf with spots on it, which turned out to be scab, a fungus. I don't use it every day. I'd use it more if I saw it actually saving me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's handy for odd jobs, like the leaf thing. I wouldn't make a big deal of it. Most people I know are in the same place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm still on not much money, in a job I like, with about three weeks of savings. My partner Leon's a mechanic at the tyre place and he earns more than me. I'd like to be paid properly for the skill, once I've got the skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get better at pruning, that's the whole year really. Derek said he'd give me a row of my own to prune this winter and he'd check it. If I can get it down to eight minutes a tree, I'd ask for a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Fine. This is basically now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest thing about pruning to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the tree two years ahead. You cut a branch now and it decides where the fruit is in two summers. Derek looks at a tree and sees the future. I look at it and see a lot of sticks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay for the car to be fixed properly, not by Leon on a Sunday with second-hand parts. And start a proper savings pot, so a broken boiler isn't a crisis.

S0.say: I'd say it's handy for odd jobs, like checking a photo of a spotted leaf. I wouldn't make a big deal of it, and most people I know feel the same.
S0.think: It means I'm still on low pay in a job I like, with about three weeks of savings. I'd like to be paid properly for the skill once I actually have it.
S0.do: Works on getting faster at pruning, aiming to cut her time from twelve to eight minutes a tree on the row Derek gives her. Asks for a raise once she reaches that speed.
S0.quote: Derek looks at a tree and sees the future. I look at it and see a lot of sticks.
S0.fieldNote: She measures her progress in minutes per tree, which gave the interview a practical feel from the start. She uses AI tools only when she has seen them save time, which fits her steady profile. Modest about her skill without being down on herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for companies, but it's a shame for people like me ten years ago. Somebody's got to give beginners a chance. Derek gave me one when I couldn't tell a pear from an apple tree in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm glad I'm already in. And if it's slow, I've got time to get good. Some tasks might go, like grading. There's already a machine that photographs every apple and sorts it by colour and size at the big packhouse. If Derek gets one, that's my November gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure I was the one who learned the grading machine if it came, once I'd seen it work at the packhouse. And keep at the pruning, because that's the part that's hardest to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit uneasy at the edges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in November if the grading went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more cold store work, or helping Derek with the farm shop stall at the market, which he hates doing. Or fewer hours. In November fewer hours would hurt, because there's Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said pruning is hardest to replace. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's what I'd like to think. Pruning is where I'm slowest and it's the one job I'd bet a machine can't do. Which probably means it'll be the first one they crack.

S1.say: I'd say it makes sense for companies but it's a shame for beginners. Somebody has to give them a chance, like Derek gave me.
S1.think: I'm glad I'm already in, and slow change gives me time to get good. Grading might go to a machine that photographs and sorts every apple, which would take my November work.
S1.do: Learns the grading machine if Derek buys one, after seeing it work at the big packhouse. Keeps building her pruning skill and takes on market stall or cold store work if grading hours go.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little uneasy at the edges.
S1.quote: Pruning is where I'm slowest and it's the one job I'd bet a machine can't do. Which probably means it'll be the first one they crack.
S1.fieldNote: When I gently questioned her confidence about pruning, she turned it on herself with a sharp, funny line. Her plan follows her steady style: see the machine work elsewhere, then learn it. Christmas came up as the pinch point in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard on office people and the government needs to help them retrain, but sensibly, not throwing money around. I'd stay out of arguments online. They never change anyone's mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it doesn't touch the orchard much. Derek does his own accounts and he'd love an assistant to do them, so maybe that's one good thing. My worry is Leon, actually not him, his boss. The tyre place could put all the bookings on an AI, and the receptionist, Jen, would be gone. She's Leon's sister.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. Maybe help Derek set up an assistant for the accounts and the spray records, if he asked, because I'm better with phones than him. Keep doing the pruning and the picking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Jen. Fine for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen with Jen if she lost the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably come and pick apples in autumn, honestly, there's always work in picking for six weeks. It's not the same money. She's got two kids and her ex doesn't help, so it'd be bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said retraining but 'sensibly'. What does sensible look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid courses that end in a real job, not courses for the sake of it. Jen did a course once, in social media, and it got her nothing. I'd want the company that cut her job to pay part of it.

S2.say: I'd say it will be hard on office workers and the government needs to help them retrain, but sensibly. I'd stay out of online arguments because they never change minds.
S2.think: It doesn't touch the orchard much, and Derek would love an assistant for his accounts. My worry is Leon's sister Jen, the receptionist at the tyre place, whose job could go to an AI booking system.
S2.do: Offers to help Derek set up an AI assistant for his accounts and spray records. Carries on pruning and picking, and points Jen toward six weeks of apple picking if she loses her job.
S2.feel: Uneasy for Jen, fine for herself.
S2.quote: She'd probably come and pick apples in autumn, honestly, there's always work in picking for six weeks. It's not the same money.
S2.fieldNote: Her concern landed on a specific person, her partner's sister, a single mother on reception. Her view of retraining was practical and centrist: real jobs at the end, partly paid by the company. She'd happily be the one who sets up AI tools for her boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not fair if some people make a fortune while others lose everything. But I'd also say we shouldn't wreck the economy fixing it. Somewhere in between, a bit of tax and a lot of help finding work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think for me it's okay at work and worse at home. Leon and I were trying to save for a deposit on a small house. If prices boom, that's gone, years further away. I'd be renting till I'm forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay at Pearce's, for sure, because that's a physical job and those are safe in this one. Maybe ask Derek for weekend hours in the farm shop he keeps saying he'll open. Pick up extra in picking season, take the bonuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit sad. The house thing stings more than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would more office workers losing jobs change who comes to pick in autumn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. More local people, fewer from abroad maybe, people who've never picked before. Which means slower crews, more bruised fruit, and I'd be training them. Actually that might be a chance for me, being the one who shows them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leon about the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we stop pretending we'll buy in three years. Make it ten. Then maybe it doesn't feel like failing every month. He'd be quiet about it. He wanted his own garage, that's his dream.

S3.say: I'd say it isn't fair for some to make a fortune while others lose everything, but we shouldn't wreck the economy fixing it. A bit of tax and a lot of help finding work.
S3.think: For me it's okay at work and worse at home. Leon and I were saving for a deposit, and booming prices would push buying a house years away.
S3.do: Stays at Pearce Orchards and asks for weekend hours in the farm shop Derek plans to open. Takes extra picking-season work and bonuses, and offers to train new local pickers.
S3.feel: Uneasy and a little sad, with the house worry stinging more than she expected.
S3.quote: That we stop pretending we'll buy in three years. Make it ten. Then maybe it doesn't feel like failing every month.
S3.fieldNote: She spotted a new chance in the picking crews: laid-off locals who would need training. The house deposit was her real loss, and she reframed it calmly rather than raging about it. Her policy answer stayed firmly in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks for staying with me. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I want to see it before I believe it. There are apple-picking robots already, with suction arms that pull the fruit off, but last I heard they were slow and bruised the Galas. If they work, they work. I'd say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think pickers go first, then grading, then the tractor work. Pruning maybe last. I'd be one person left doing the bits the machines can't, or I'd be gone. Derek's sixty and tired, and if a robot company offered to run the picking for him, he'd say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and see a robot working on a real orchard, first thing, before Derek buys one. Then ask him straight whether he's planning it. If he is, I'd ask to be trained to look after them, maybe a course paid by the robot company. And I'd start looking at jobs in the town just in case, care work or the hospital, though that sounds like robots too now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Properly anxious. It's the first one where I can picture an orchard with nobody in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work 'sounds like robots too now'. Where would you go if everything hands-on is touched?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. That's the bit with no answer. Maybe the thing is to be the person who fixes the machines, like Leon fixes cars. He says if robots come, someone's got to change their tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would picking season look like with robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet. No radios in the rows, no lunch on the bins with the crew, no Bulgarian guys teaching me card games. Just whirring. I'd miss the people more than the work.

S4.say: I'd say I want to see it before I believe it, because the apple-picking robots I've heard of were slow and bruised the fruit. If they work, they work.
S4.think: Pickers go first, then grading, then tractor work, with pruning maybe last. Derek is sixty and tired, and he'd say yes if a robot company offered to run his picking.
S4.do: Visits a working robot orchard before Derek buys anything and asks him directly about his plans. Asks to be trained to look after the robots, ideally on a course paid by the robot company, and quietly looks at jobs in town.
S4.feel: Properly anxious for the first time, able to picture an empty orchard.
S4.quote: No radios in the rows, no lunch on the bins with the crew, no Bulgarian guys teaching me card games. Just whirring. I'd miss the people more than the work.
S4.fieldNote: Her steady instinct held: see it working first, then decide. She mapped the order she'd expect tasks to go, which showed how much she'd thought about it. What she said she'd miss most was the people, not the job or the pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because it's the only one where the orchard itself changes. What would help is time to see them working first, and training paid for by whoever's selling them. And keeping some people on, even if it costs a bit. An orchard needs someone who knows the trees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the seasonal crew. They're the ones who'd lose most, and they won't be in your study because they're only here six weeks. Somebody should ask them.

headlineQuote: Pruning is where I'm slowest and it's the one job I'd bet a machine can't do. Which probably means it'll be the first one they crack.
portrait: Sara Olsen is a 27-year-old orchard worker on a sixty-hectare apple and pear farm, still slow at pruning and measuring her progress in minutes per tree. She lives with her partner Leon, a mechanic, has about three weeks of savings, and uses AI tools only when she has seen them save time. Through the office scenarios her worry lands on Leon's sister and on their fading hope of a house deposit. With robots she becomes properly anxious but stays practical: see one working, ask her boss directly, and ask to be trained. Her politics sit in the middle, and what she'd miss most is the picking crew.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because it's the only one where the orchard itself changes and she can picture it empty.
whatWouldHelp: Time to see robots working before they arrive, training paid for by the robot sellers, and farms keeping some people who know the trees.
